title: Generic data types
summary: Removing duplication with type parameters: generic functions, structs, enums and methods, methods for one concrete type, const generics, and why generics cost nothing at run time.

sections: TRPL 10 Removing Duplication by Extracting a Function
TRPL 10.1 Performance of Code Using Generics
PR ch11 Generic Functions and Type Parameters

blocks.md:
You already use generics every day: `Vec<T>`, `Option<T>` and `Result<T, E>` work for any `T`. In this chapter you write your own. The goal is the same as for functions: **write a piece of logic once** and reuse it, here across many **types** instead of many values.

*The Rust Programming Language* starts with plain duplication. Two functions find the largest number and the largest character in a slice; their bodies are identical, only the types differ:

blocks.title: A generic function
blocks.md:
To merge them, give the function a **type parameter** in angle brackets after its name, conventionally a short name like `T`, and use it where the concrete type was:

```rust
fn largest<T>(list: &[T]) -> &T {
```

Read it as "`largest` is generic over some type `T`; it takes a slice of `T` and returns a reference to a `T`." But this alone does not compile:

blocks.output:
error[E0369]: binary operation `>` cannot be applied to type `&T`
 --> src/main.rs:4:17
  |
4 |         if item > largest {
  |            ---- ^ ------- &T
  |            |
  |            &T
  |
help: consider restricting type parameter `T` with trait `PartialOrd`
  |
1 | fn largest<T: std::cmp::PartialOrd>(list: &[T]) -> &T {
  |             ++++++++++++++++++++++
blocks.explain: Inside the body, the compiler only lets you do with `T` what is true of **every** possible `T`. Not every type can be compared with `>`. The help line shows the fix: a **trait bound** saying `T` must be comparable. Lesson 2 explains traits; for now, copy the bound.
One function, four types. The compiler infers `T` from the argument at each call.

blocks.title: Generic structs and enums
blocks.md: Structs can have type parameters too. Declare them after the struct name and use them in the fields:

blocks.explain: With one parameter, `x` and `y` must be the **same** type: `Point { x: 5, y: 4.0 }` is a type mismatch. Use two parameters, as in `Pair<T, U>`, when they may differ. Many type parameters make code hard to read; if you need a lot, the type may want splitting.

blocks.title: Generic methods
blocks.md: To write methods for a generic struct, declare the parameter after `impl` too: `impl<T> Point<T>`. The first `<T>` introduces the name; the second uses it. You can also write an `impl` block for one **concrete** type: those methods exist only for that type.

blocks.title: Methods with their own parameters
blocks.md: A method can introduce type parameters of its own, separate from the struct's. *The Rust Programming Language* shows `fn mixup<X2, Y2>(self, other: Point<X2, Y2>) -> Point<X1, Y2>`, which takes `x` from one point and `y` from another, possibly of different types.

blocks.title: Const generics
blocks.md: Type parameters stand for types. **Const generics** stand for values, usually array lengths: `[T; N]` is generic over the number `N`. Declare one with `const N: usize`:

blocks.title: Monomorphization: what the compiler does with generics

steps.title: You write one generic definition
steps.md: The compiler type-checks it once, using only what the bounds promise about `T`.

steps.title: It collects every concrete use
steps.md: Your program calls `largest` with `i32` and with `char`.
steps.code:
largest(&[34, 50, 25]);   // T = i32
largest(&['y', 'm']);     // T = char

steps.title: It stamps out one copy per type
steps.md: Behind the scenes there are now two ordinary, specialized functions. This is **monomorphization** ("making single-form"). The same happens to `Option<i32>` and `Option<f64>`.

steps.title: No run-time cost
steps.md: Each copy is compiled and optimized for its type, so generic code runs exactly as fast as code you wrote by hand. The price is paid at compile time and in binary size. Chapter 18's trait objects make the opposite trade.

blocks.title: A generic Stack
blocks.md: `Stack` only holds `i32`. Make it generic over `T` so the same code works for strings, then add a `peek` method returning `Option<&T>`.

blocks.title: Generic helpers
blocks.goal: Write generic functions and a generic struct with bounds and a concrete-type impl.
blocks.behavior:
- `pub fn largest<T: PartialOrd>(list: &[T]) -> Option<&T>`: the largest element, or `None` for an empty slice.
- `pub fn count_matching<T: PartialEq>(list: &[T], target: &T) -> usize`: how many elements equal `target`.
- `pub struct Pair<T> { pub a: T, pub b: T }` with:
  - `pub fn new(a: T, b: T) -> Self`
  - `pub fn swap(self) -> Pair<T>` (a and b exchanged)
  - `pub fn larger(&self) -> &T` where `T: PartialOrd` (the larger of the two; `a` on a tie). Put this one in its own `impl<T: PartialOrd> Pair<T>` block.
- `impl Pair<f64> { pub fn mean(&self) -> f64 }`: only for floats.
hints: `let mut best = list.first()?;` gives `None` for an empty slice.
`list.iter().filter(|x| *x == target).count()` counts matches (or use a loop).
`impl<T: PartialOrd> Pair<T> { pub fn larger(&self) -> &T { if self.b > self.a { &self.b } else { &self.a } } }`
blocks.solution_explain: `swap` takes `self` by value so it can move both fields into the new pair without needing `T: Clone`. Putting `larger` in a block with a bound means `Pair<T>` can still hold types that cannot be compared; they just do not get that method.

questions.q: Why does `fn biggest<T>(a: T, b: T) -> T { if a > b { a } else { b } }` not compile?
options: Not every type supports `>`; T needs a `PartialOrd` bound
Two parameters cannot share a type
questions.explanation: A generic body may only use what every T can do.

questions.q: With `struct Point<T> { x: T, y: T }`, what is `Point { x: 1, y: 2.5 }`?
options: A type error: x and y must be the same type
questions.explanation: Use two type parameters if they may differ.

questions.q: What does `impl Point<f32> { fn norm(&self) -> f32 { ... } }` mean?
questions.explanation: An impl for a concrete type adds methods only to that type.

options: Generating a specialized copy of generic code for each concrete type used
Converting all types to one type
questions.explanation: It is why generics have no run-time cost.

questions.q: Complete the header for methods on a generic struct: `impl___ Point<T> { ... }`

points: Type parameters (`<T>`) let one function, struct, enum or method work for many types.
A generic body can only use what its bounds promise, such as `T: PartialOrd` for `>`.
`impl<T> Point<T>` adds methods for every T; `impl Point<f64>` only for that type.
Const generics (`const N: usize`) parameterize over values like array lengths.
Monomorphization makes generic code as fast as hand-written specialized code.

terms.def: Code written with type parameters so it works for many concrete types.
A placeholder for a type, like T in fn largest<T>(list: &[T]), filled in at each use.
The compiler generating a specialized copy of generic code for each concrete type it is used with.
A generic parameter that stands for a constant value, written const N: usize.
